title: Wilson signs ordinance banning AI, data-driven price changes at grocery stores
source_used: KOMO News (full article, from the prefetched text)
key_facts: Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson signed the Fair and Transparent Pricing ordinance into law on Monday 5 Oct 2026, following a 7-2 approval from the Seattle City Council; the city calls it the first of its kind in the nation.

Large grocers, defined as chains with at least 20 locations worldwide, may not base prices on personal details, browsing history, social media activity or chatbot conversations, and must clearly post prices available to all customers.

The rules cover in-person and online grocery retailers and delivery services; traditional discounts, open coupons and savings for groups such as seniors and veterans are still allowed; small grocers, convenience stores and farmers' markets are not affected.

The law was partly inspired by 2025 consumer investigations that found price differences for the same groceries; one report found people using an app at the same Safeway in South Seattle at the same time saw up to a 23% gap between the lowest and highest price for the same item.

Councilmember Alexis Mercedes Rinck, who worked on the measure with Wilson, said it is meant to put guardrails on what big businesses do with personal information and to prevent 'AI-assisted price gouging'.

The Northwest Grocery Retail Association's Amanda Dalton called it an 'untested policy' that could mean fewer coupons, discounts and savings, and said loyalty programs could go away in Seattle; Safeway said it does not use shopper information to set higher prices but uses customer data for digital coupons and member prices.

Councilmember Maritza Rivera voted against: she supports banning price rises based on personal data but fears stores will offer fewer discounts; the grocery workers' union UFCW 3000 plans to push for similar rules at state level.

Under the rules, large grocers—defined as chains with at least 20 locations worldwide—will not be allowed to base prices on personal details, browsing history, social media activity, or chatbot conversations.

why_it_matters_hint: A first-of-its-kind city law stops big grocery chains from tailoring prices to shoppers' personal data; grocers call it untested and warn it could cost shoppers discounts.
event_date: 5 Oct 2026 (signed); the council vote date is not stated in the article
